You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
The failing test `testContainsIgnoreCase_LocaleIndependence` tests `StringUtils.containsIgnoreCase` for correctness across different locales including English, Turkish (locale "tr"), and the default locale. The test inputs include some tricky case pairs such as different cases of "i" and Greek character sigmas. It expects the case-insensitive contains check to yield expected true/false results regardless of locale.

The current bug report highlights that the use of `String.toUpperCase()` or `String.toLowerCase()` is locale-sensitive and can cause errors when used for case-insensitive string comparisons. This is a known common mistake. The bug is caused by the fact that these methods change behavior based on the JVM default locale, so the same string can produce different results for different locales. The test exposes this defect by running in different locales including Turkish, where casing rules differ from English.

Looking at the `StringUtils.containsIgnoreCase` method:
```java
public static boolean containsIgnoreCase(String str, String searchStr) {
    if (str == null || searchStr == null) {
        return false;
    }
    return contains(str.toUpperCase(), searchStr.toUpperCase());
}
```
We see that it converts both the source string and the search string to uppercase using the platform default locale (no locale param provided in `toUpperCase()`) and then checks whether one contains the other.

This is the root cause of the failure. In some locales like Turkish, the uppercase mapping of certain characters differs from English (e.g., 'i' uppercases to a different character than 'I'). So the strings `tdata[j][0]` and `tdata[j][1]` which should match ignoring case fail because the uppercase transformation is locale-dependent.

The correct approach to perform locale-independent case insensitive string comparisons is to specify a fixed locale (often `Locale.ENGLISH` or `Locale.ROOT`) in the calls to `toUpperCase` or `toLowerCase`. Alternatively, other locale-independent comparison techniques can be used.

Summary:
- The root cause of the bug is the use of locale-sensitive `String.toUpperCase()` in `StringUtils.containsIgnoreCase`.
- Different JVM default locales cause inconsistent behavior breaking locale-independent case-insensitive tests.
- The failing test exactly exposes this by testing in different locales including Turkish.
- The fix would be to modify `containsIgnoreCase` to use locale-independent uppercase/lowercase, e.g., `toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT)`.

The recent unrelated bug reports can be ignored here because they do not relate to string comparison or locale issues.

Hence the diagnosis is that `StringUtils.containsIgnoreCase` uses locale-sensitive `toUpperCase()` which leads to failures in locale-independent case ignore tests when default locale is not English.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
